newsitem.title: CONGO: Airport battle rages at heart of Congo civil war.
newsitem.headline: Airport battle rages at heart of Congo civil war.

text.p: Congo's civil war enemies wrestled for control of Brazzaville airport on Thursday, with both trumpeting victory while shells rained down for a second day.
Artillery thundered around Maya-Maya airport a day after former Marxist leader Denis Sassou Nguesso launched an assault to snatch it from President Pascal Lissouba.
The international Red Cross (ICRC), the only aid agency at work in the capital, said its handful of foreign staff were leaving as the situation deteriorated.

"We are not completely withdrawing but our expatriates are leaving. Our local staff will continue working," spokesman Paolo dell'Oca said in the twin city of Kinshasa across the Congo river in former Zaire.
Some of the expatriates left by speedboat for Kinshasa.
Wednesday's duel killed off a dying week-old truce. It had dampened clashes but failed to make city streets safe enough for the Red Cross to clean them of scores of rotting bodies.
It also dashed hopes of a swift deployment of a planned U.N. peacekeeping force whose arrival was made dependent on a firm truce and a demilitarised airport.
Clashes extended for the first time to a neutral part of the city controlled by Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas.
A spokesman said 60 shells landed in his area, one crashing into a hospital operating theatre and killing a woman and the child she was giving birth to.
Kolelas hosted fresh mediation talks with military leaders from both sides on Thursday as the war went on.
In a joint declaration all sides agreed that peace and the rule of law were needed, but failed to arrange a cessation of hostilities.
Fighting has cut the city down the middle since early June and is now centred on the strategically important airport, about five km (three miles) from the centre.
Losing it would be a big blow to Lissouba, but Kinshasa airline officials who spoke to Brazzaville control tower by radio said they were told his forces were still in place.
"The airport is well and truly in the hands of the regular army," a Lissouba aide told Reuters by telephone.
"There was an incursion yesterday but it was repulsed and Sassou's bandits abandoned a tank with some dead in it."
A Sassou spokesman disagreed.
"Maya-Maya has been under the control of General Sassou's partisans since yesterday afternoon," he said by telephone from their northern suburbs stronghold. "We're at war."
Hundreds of civilians have been fleeing Brazzaville to safer suburbs on its northern and southern edges.
French troops evacuated thousands of foreigners through the airport after the fighting began, but pulled out last week. Paris said it would not send soldiers to an intervention force.
Paris protested on Thursday after panicky government troops assaulted its ambassador Raymond Cesaire, beat up his bodyguard and shot at escorts as they left Lissouba's palace after talks.

Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left, said he would carry on working from his embassy, 200 metres (yards) from the front line. Outside the compound, soldiers carted off TV sets and other booty as they looted homes and shops.
Sassou, for 13 years Congo's one-party president until Lissouba defeated him in free elections in 1992, was to have run in next month's presidential elections.
The poll, in which he, Lissouba and Kolelas were main contenders, has been postponed. All three men control their own private militias.
